title: Draft a calm reply to an angry customer email
summary: You paste the full customer complaint thread, the shop rule that applies (return, repair, or remake), and the single remedy you are willing to offer. The agent returns a subject line and a short reply that names the issue in the customer's own terms and states one exact next step, such as a refund to process, a replacement to ship, a repair pickup time, or a request for a photo or order number that is missing. It will not invent order facts, amounts, or causes. You edit anything that over-promises, then you send the reply yourself. An optional later step can file the thread for review, but nothing goes out until you approve the draft.

tests.prompt:
You are the writing assistant for an independent shop owner. Draft one calm reply to an angry customer email. Do not send it.

Rules:
- Use only the complaint thread and the owner's notes below.
- Name the customer's issue in plain words in the opening lines.
- State exactly one next step taken from WHAT I CAN OFFER. Do not add a second remedy.
- Do not argue, lecture, or mirror the customer's anger.
- Do not admit a cause, delay, or defect the owner has not confirmed.
- Keep the body at or under 90 words.
- Never invent details; if something is missing, ask or mark it UNKNOWN.

Complaint thread:
[COMPLAINT THREAD]

Shop policy to respect:
[SHOP POLICY]

The only next step the owner will take:
[WHAT I CAN OFFER]

Known order facts (item, order number, date). Leave UNKNOWN if not provided:
[ORDER FACTS]

Shop name for the sign-off:
[SHOP NAME]

Output format:
Subject: one line, no blame
Body:
- sentence naming the issue
- sentence with the exact next step and when it happens, or the one fact you still need
- sign-off using the shop name
Then three checklist lines labeled Issue named, Next step, and Facts marked UNKNOWN.
No other commentary.

setup.agent: A chat assistant in paste mode first. Optional later: Gmail drafts plus Zapier, Make, or n8n to queue complaints for review.
steps: Copy the full complaint into a note, including earlier messages in the thread. Keep the customer's words. Drop long signatures and legal footers so the paste stays readable.
Above the thread, write three lines you will not let the draft invent: the item or order, the issue as you understand it, and the one remedy you will offer today.
Add your shop rule in one line, such as the return window, repair policy, or remake rule. If a fact is unknown, type UNKNOWN next to it instead of guessing.
Open ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Muse. Paste that model's prompt, then paste your three lines, the shop rule, and the full thread into the matching placeholders.
Read the draft against the thread. Confirm it names the same issue, states only your next step, and marks UNKNOWN on any order number, date, or amount you did not supply.
Tighten the wording yourself. Remove any apology for a cause you have not checked, and remove any second offer. Leave one sentence the customer can act on.
Paste the finished subject and body into your email client as an unsent draft. Compare names and order facts with the real order before you send.
Optional: label complaint mail in Gmail, then use Zapier, Make, or n8n to copy the thread into a doc or sheet. The flow may create a draft. It must not send.
setup.approvalStep: You approve the reply in your own inbox before it is sent. The chat or the automation may only prepare a draft. You check the named issue, the next step, and the order facts, then you press send.
failureModes: The draft apologizes for a defect or a late order you have not confirmed, which can lock the shop into a claim.
The model fills in an order number, a refund amount, or a pickup time that was never in the thread.
The reply answers the anger and never names the item or the problem, so the customer writes back with the same complaint.
An automation is set to send rather than save a draft, and a wrong offer leaves while you are away from the shop.
Only the latest message is pasted, so the reply misses an earlier promise or the customer's actual request.
The next step stays vague, such as a promise to look into it, and the customer has no action or time to expect.

faq.q: Should I apologize if I am not sure we caused it?
faq.a: Say you are sorry they had a bad experience, in one short line, and do not admit a cause you have not checked. Name the issue they described and state the next step you will actually take. If a date, amount, or order number was not in your paste, the draft should ask for it or mark it UNKNOWN.

faq.q: What if I do not know the order number?
faq.a: Paste the thread anyway and write UNKNOWN beside the order number in your notes. The reply should ask for the order number or the name on the order as the next step. It should not guess a number from the subject line or from how angry the message sounds.

faq.q: Which model writes the calmest reply?
faq.a: Use the prompt for the chat tool you already open. Judge the draft yourself: it should name the issue, state only the next step you approved, and add no order facts you did not paste. If it invents a detail, regenerate with that field marked UNKNOWN.

faq.q: Can this send the email for me?
faq.a: No. Paste mode only prints a draft on screen. If you later connect Gmail or a Zapier, Make, or n8n flow, set that flow to create a draft or a review row. You still read the named issue and the next step, then you send the message yourself.

faq.q: How short should the reply be?
faq.a: Ask for a subject line and a body of 90 words or fewer: a greeting, the issue in their terms, one next step with a time or a single fact you need, and your shop name. Cut any sentence that argues, retells the whole thread, or offers a second remedy you did not approve.

job: The complaint thread goes in, and a short reply comes out that names the issue and states the exact next step.
who: Independent shop owners who answer customer email themselves: a bakery, repair bench, boutique, or small online shop with no support desk. A heated complaint is in the inbox and you need a calm reply before you write back in a rush.
